Family Health

Bladder pain syndrome: assessment and treatment choices

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Interstitial cystitis, also called bladder pain syndrome or IC/BPS, can make ordinary plans revolve around pain and the next toilet visit. Care aims to reduce that burden and improve sleep, activity and comfort. There is no treatment that reliably cures everyone, but a considered combination of options can help. The starting point is a careful assessment, followed by a plan that is reviewed rather than continued automatically.

What makes this a bladder-pain condition

Pain, pressure or discomfort may build as the bladder fills and ease for a while after passing urine. Frequent small voids, urgency even soon after a toilet visit, and waking at night are common descriptions. Pain may be felt in the lower abdomen, pelvis, back or genital area, and sex or ejaculation can be uncomfortable.

Symptoms range from mild to severe and may fluctuate or disappear for a time before returning. A particular daily number of toilet visits does not diagnose IC/BPS. It occurs in women and men; being younger than a typical patient does not rule it out. Describe how the symptoms differ from your usual pattern and what they prevent you from doing.

The cause is uncertain, and one negative test is not a diagnosis

Changes in the bladder lining, inflammation, immune activity and altered pain signalling are possible contributors. Pelvic-floor tension and other long-term pain conditions can coexist. These possibilities do not identify a single cause in every person, and a flare after stress does not mean that the pain is invented or your fault.

IC/BPS is different from an ordinary bacterial bladder infection. Clinicians may use a definition involving bladder-related symptoms lasting more than six weeks without infection or another identifiable cause, but duration alone is insufficient. Do not wait six weeks to seek help. Infection, stones, genital or prostate conditions, endometriosis and other explanations need consideration according to the history.

Build an assessment around the questions that matter

Bring previous urine results, medicines, treatment responses and a short bladder diary. Record drinking, toilet visits, approximate amounts if requested, pain before and after emptying, and any bleeding or sexual symptoms. Examination may include the abdomen and pelvic-floor muscles, with explanation, consent and a chaperone if wanted.

Urinalysis and a urine culture may help assess infection or blood. A bladder scan for urine remaining after emptying is useful when poor emptying is suspected; this is measured after urination, not after a bowel movement. STI testing, imaging or other investigations answer selected questions. Not everyone needs the same cancer, prostate, biopsy or pressure-testing panel, and a symptom questionnaire cannot establish the diagnosis alone.

Why a cystoscopy or Hunner lesion can change the plan

Cystoscopy uses a small camera to inspect the bladder. It may help investigate bleeding, uncertain findings or suspected Hunner lesions: distinct inflamed areas of the bladder lining. These lesions can guide specific treatment. Tiny bleeding spots called glomerulations are not, by themselves, a reliable diagnostic sign. A suspicious area may need a biopsy to exclude another condition.

Guidelines differ on how routinely to perform cystoscopy. The AUA recommends it for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected Hunner lesions, while the 2025 Canadian guideline supports broader use. Discuss the purpose, comfort measures and anaesthesia options with the urologist. Pressure testing and stretching the bladder are separate procedures; neither is an automatic requirement merely because symptoms have persisted.

Look for personal triggers without making life smaller

A food-and-symptom record may reveal that a particular drink or food repeatedly worsens discomfort. Possible triggers include coffee or other caffeinated drinks, alcohol, fizzy drinks, citrus, tomatoes, chocolate, spicy foods and artificial sweeteners. These are possibilities, not a list everyone must eliminate. Try manageable changes and consider a dietitian if restrictions are growing.

Agree on an appropriate fluid intake rather than deliberately dehydrating yourself or forcing large volumes. Comfortable clothing, adapted activity, sleep support and relaxation may help you manage flares. Smoking cessation supports general health and may reduce bladder irritation. Keep room for activities and relationships that matter to you; symptom management should have practical goals beyond avoiding every possible trigger.

Pelvic-floor care and bladder training need tailoring

When the pelvic floor is tender or overactive, a specialist physiotherapist may work on relaxation, stretching and manual treatment. Repeated strengthening squeezes can be the wrong approach for this pattern. Do not start an intensive Kegel routine simply because the symptoms involve the bladder; the examination should guide the exercises.

Bladder training may be useful under professional guidance, but it is not an instruction to force yourself through escalating pain or jump to a fixed holding interval. Agree on a tolerable approach and how to adjust it during flares. Pain-management or psychological support can sit alongside bladder treatment, helping with sleep, distress and daily function without dismissing physical symptoms.

Oral medicines are options to discuss, not a fixed ladder

Amitriptyline may be offered to modify pain symptoms; its use does not imply that the problem is depression. Sleepiness, dry mouth, constipation, dizziness and difficulty urinating can limit treatment. Review benefit and adverse effects with the prescriber. A medicine that makes emptying harder is not something to keep increasing without advice.

Hydroxyzine, an antihistamine, is another possible option, but evidence of benefit is mixed and it is not a guaranteed remedy for night-time urination. Heart-rhythm risks and interacting medicines require checking. Other oral choices depend on the symptom pattern and local practice. Ask what improvement to expect, how long a reasonable trial lasts and how to stop or change an ineffective treatment safely.

Pentosan requires a separate discussion about benefit and vision

Pentosan polysulfate, sold as Elmiron, is used for bladder pain in some settings, but recommendations differ. The AUA lists it as an option and the EAU supports its use; the 2025 Canadian guideline conditionally recommends against it because expected benefit is small and potential harms matter. This disagreement makes an individual benefits-and-risks discussion essential, including whether it has helped someone already taking it.

Pentosan has been associated with retinal pigment changes that may be irreversible and can progress after stopping. Discuss eye history before treatment and arrange baseline and periodic retinal assessment according to the product guidance and eye specialist. Promptly report blurred vision, difficulty reading or slow adjustment to dim light. Bleeding risk, other medicines, pregnancy and breastfeeding also need review. Do not start it, change the amount or abandon monitoring based on a general article.

Bladder instillations deliver medicine through a catheter

An instillation places a prescribed liquid into the bladder for a planned period before it is released. DMSO, lidocaine, heparin and different combinations are used in selected settings. Evidence does not identify one mixture as best for everyone. Ask about likely benefit, repeat visits, catheter discomfort, infection risk and what would lead the team to change the plan.

DMSO can temporarily irritate the bladder and cause a garlic-like taste or odour. Its prescribing information also calls for appropriate eye and laboratory monitoring and a review of other medicines. It is a clinical bladder treatment, not an invitation to use industrial DMSO, swallow it or apply an improvised mixture. Discuss pregnancy or breastfeeding before treatment; symptom relief is not a treatment for bacterial infection.

Procedures should have a clear target

If Hunner lesions are present, treatment may involve cauterising them or injecting a steroid into the lesion. This is different from taking long-term oral steroids for nonspecific bladder pain. Symptoms may recur, so follow-up remains necessary. A urologist can explain why a particular lesion treatment is suitable and whether a tissue sample is needed.

Low-pressure, short-duration hydrodistension under anaesthesia is an option in some care pathways, but any relief may be temporary and recommendations differ on using it alone. Botox injections or nerve stimulation may be considered for selected persistent symptoms. Botox can cause difficulty emptying, sometimes requiring intermittent catheterisation, as well as infection. Discuss that possibility before agreeing to the procedure rather than assuming every treatment only reduces urgency.

More intensive treatment needs a careful review

Cyclosporine suppresses immune activity and is sometimes considered for difficult cases, particularly certain patients with Hunner lesions. Evidence remains limited, and specialist guidance differs. Kidney injury, high blood pressure and other adverse effects mean that close monitoring is essential. It is not an automatic final medicine for anyone whose earlier treatment failed.

Major surgery to enlarge or remove the bladder or divert urine is uncommon and reserved for carefully selected severe disease. It has substantial risks and cannot guarantee that pain will disappear. Before an irreversible procedure, revisit the diagnosis, other sources of pain, previous treatment trials and the outcomes that matter to you. Pain support should continue even when a bladder-directed option has not worked.

Keep a review plan, and act on new warning signs

Agree on measurable goals such as fewer disrupted nights, longer comfortable outings or less pain, and a date to assess progress. If benefit is absent, the team should reconsider the treatment and sometimes the diagnosis. Flares can occur, but neither a promise that half of cases resolve spontaneously nor a fixed timetable predicts your course.

Seek urgent advice for blood in the urine, fever or shivering with bladder/back pain, rapidly worsening symptoms or suspected urinary infection during pregnancy. Inability to pass urine or severe abdominal pain needs immediate care. Confusion, unusual drowsiness or difficulty speaking with suspected infection needs emergency help. A known bladder-pain diagnosis does not exclude a new infection, blockage or another urgent problem.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Discuss the purpose of each test and whether the result would change the care plan.

For each treatment, agree on expected benefit, monitoring, a review date and what to do during a flare.

Guidelines differ on some options, particularly pentosan and cystoscopy; ask how local recommendations and personal risks apply.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to organise bladder-pattern notes, previous results, treatment responses and questions for your care team. It cannot diagnose IC/BPS, interpret a bladder examination or select a medicine, instillation or operation.

When to seek help

Blood in urine, fever or shivering with pain, rapid worsening or suspected infection in pregnancy needs urgent advice. Inability to urinate or severe abdominal pain needs immediate care; confusion, unusual drowsiness or speech difficulty with suspected infection needs emergency help. Report vision changes while taking pentosan and follow the agreed monitoring plan.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Bladder-filling pain and temporary relief after emptying are useful clues, not a diagnosis on their own.
  • Assessment and Hunner-lesion findings can change which treatments are appropriate.
  • Use personal trigger information and tailored pelvic care instead of blanket restrictions or forced holding.
  • Review medicine and procedure benefits alongside retinal, bleeding, emptying and other relevant risks.
  • New bleeding, fever, retention or marked illness needs assessment rather than being assumed to be a flare.

Frequently asked questions

What is interstitial cystitis?

It is a long-term bladder-associated pain condition, often called bladder pain syndrome. It commonly involves urgency and frequent urination, after assessment has considered infection and other explanations. It is not another name for every episode of bacterial cystitis.

What symptoms can occur?

Pressure or pain may increase with bladder filling and ease briefly after emptying. Frequent small voids, night-time visits, pelvic or genital discomfort and painful sex can occur. Describe your pattern rather than diagnosing it from a set number of visits.

Is the pain always severe?

No. Severity and frequency vary, and symptoms may improve then return. The impact on sleep, work, activity and relationships matters even when the pain is not constant.

What causes bladder pain syndrome?

The exact cause is uncertain. Bladder-lining changes, inflammation, immune activity and pain signalling may contribute, with pelvic-floor or other pain conditions sometimes overlapping. A possible trigger does not prove the underlying mechanism.

Must everyone have a cystoscopy?

Practice differs. It is particularly important when bleeding, uncertain findings or suspected Hunner lesions could change care. Ask why it is being recommended for you and whether a biopsy or other procedure is planned.

Can I just hold urine longer or do more Kegels?

Do not force painful holding or start repeated strengthening without assessment. Bladder training should be tolerable and guided, while a tender, overactive pelvic floor may need relaxation-focused physiotherapy.

Why are eye checks discussed with Elmiron?

Pentosan has been associated with retinal changes that may persist or progress after treatment stops. Discuss baseline and continuing retinal assessment, and report new reading difficulty, blurred vision or trouble adapting to dim light promptly.

Does an unsuccessful treatment mean nothing can help?

No. Review the diagnosis, what the treatment targeted, its duration and any adverse effects. Another combination of support or treatment may be more appropriate, but neither a procedure nor surgery can promise a cure.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
